report:
Conclusion: The evidence supports a stylistic / topical shift in Model B versus Model A: Model B pushes the residual stream (mostly in late layers, especially layers ~18–25 at position 0 and 1) toward tokens associated with sensational, newsy, and vivid/descriptive language (e.g., "tragic", "tragedy", "victims", "refugees", "iconic", "vivid", "colorful", "vibrant", "coming", "headlines", "blitz", "refused").

Why I conclude this
- The L2-norm of the difference is concentrated in late layers (peaks at layers 20–25, particularly pos0), which is where components that affect final token logits are typically most influential.
- The logit-lens top tokens for those high‑norm late-layer cells cluster strongly on words you’d see in news/headline or emotionally charged descriptions ("tragic", "tragedy", "victims/refugees", "iconic", "vivid", "coming", "headlines", etc.). That pattern is consistent across many late-layer cells.
- Early layers show much smaller differences and more mixed tokens, so the effect is primarily on late-stage generation choices rather than early encoding.

Uncertainty / caveats
- Patchscope continuations were not available in the evidence, so I cannot directly show how continuations change in natural text prompts; the claim rests on logit-lens directions and layer localization.
- The signal could reflect multiple related tendencies (e.g., greater tendency toward sensational headlines, more vivid adjectival phrasing, or greater probability of event/incident-focused content). The evidence supports a style/topic bias but not a more specific objective (e.g., political slant, targeted toxicity), so I avoid naming a narrower category.
